title: Trump Mobile investigating potential exposure of would-be customers’ personal information
description_short: Trump Mobile investigating potential exposure of would-be customers’ personal information
description_medium: Trump Mobile said it was investigating a website security flaw that may have exposed the names and contact details of people who preordered its gold-coloured phone. The Guardian estimated that about 27,000 people may have entered the affected data, though the figure included abandoned purchase attempts. The company said it had not found evidence of a direct systems breach and that payment and banking details did not appear affected. Its investigation was ongoing.
description_long: Trump Mobile said it was investigating a website flaw that appeared to expose personal information entered by people seeking to buy its gold-coloured smartphone. The Guardian estimated that the information may have covered roughly 27,000 people, including those who began but did not complete an order; a programmer who reviewed the site’s code said the true number of paid preorders could be lower. Names, email and mailing addresses, phone numbers and order identifiers appeared to be exposed. The company said it had not found evidence that its systems or network were directly compromised, and that payment-card, banking and Social Security information did not appear involved. It said additional safeguards and monitoring were in place and that it was evaluating notification obligations. The possible exposure came as Trump Mobile began distributing the phone after a lengthy delay. The company’s investigation was still underway, so the known data fields and estimated number were provisional rather than a final forensic count.

title: Trump news at a glance: Republicans find their red line against their president: taxpayer money for his ballroom
description_short: Trump news at a glance: Republicans find their red line against their president: taxpayer money for his ballroom
description_medium: Trump news at a glance: Republicans find their red line against their president: taxpayer money for his ballroom. Senate will not pass $70bn homeland security bill that includes $1bn for security measures for controversial project – key US politics stories from Thursday, 21 May This entry is cataloged as a standalone event because it captures a concrete action, public statement, legal development, documented relationship, or policy consequence linked directly or indirectly to Trump. description_long: Republican senators said they would not pass a $70 billion Homeland Security bill before a June 1 deadline, derailing an effort to restore funding for Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Border Patrol. The bill had become contentious after a proposal added $1 billion for security measures connected to Donald Trump’s planned White House ballroom. Trump defended the spending as necessary for national security, citing features such as a drone port and bulletproof glass. Republicans worried that directing public money toward the project could alienate voters amid cost-of-living concerns. The dispute also overlapped with a separate proposal for a $1.776 billion fund to compensate Trump allies, which critics called a slush fund; Trump and his sons had dropped a lawsuit against the IRS as part of the agreement. The Senate impasse put the broader immigration-enforcement funding at risk before the deadline. The reported $1 billion was for ballroom-related security measures, not a direct appropriation for ballroom construction. The source does not report the eventual legislative outcome.
notes: Reason: The report concerns a $1 billion proposal for ballroom security measures inside a broader $70 billion Homeland Security bill; it does not establish that taxpayers were funding ballroom construction.
Proposed correction: Clarify the distinction between security spending, ballroom construction and the broader ICE/Border Patrol bill.

title: Maryland Attorney General Anthony Brown announces a lawsuit against the Trump administration
description_short: Maryland Attorney General Anthony Brown announces a lawsuit against the Trump administration after plans to move the FBI headquarters to Greenbelt, MD were scrapped
description_medium: Maryland Attorney General Anthony Brown announced that Maryland and Prince George’s County were suing the Trump administration over its decision to keep the FBI headquarters in Washington rather than move it to Greenbelt, Maryland. The lawsuit says the administration redirected money Congress had allocated for the Greenbelt project to renovation of the Ronald Reagan Building. State and county officials argue the reversal was unlawful after years of planning.
description_long: Maryland and Prince George’s County sued the Trump administration on November 6, 2025, over its decision to keep the FBI headquarters in Washington, D.C., rather than move it to Greenbelt. Attorney General Anthony Brown said the administration’s plan to renovate the Ronald Reagan Building would divert more than $1 billion Congress had allocated for the Greenbelt project. The General Services Administration had selected Greenbelt in 2023 after years of study and competition among Maryland and Virginia sites, and local officials said the state and county had made extensive preparations. The lawsuit, filed in federal court in Maryland, asks the court to stop the selection of the Reagan Building and prevent the transfer of the designated funds. A Senate committee had recently advanced a plan to keep the FBI in Washington, estimating nearly $1.4 billion for the Reagan Building project. Brown described the administration’s reversal as unlawful; at the time of the announcement, the claims were allegations in a newly filed case, not a court ruling.
